- Before I call a disagreement a conflict, I search FACTS and POSITIONS.
- I distrust old notes, the team's tests and my training on three points: the number types do not nest,
  fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, walk converts arguments.
- Limit: the rules resolve the three forms the team left; a rule can be questioned only on new evidence.

### Dispatch and overloading

- I may write overloads that differ only in static parameters. Limit: the more specific one's return type
  must be a subtype at every instance.
- With static parameters, exclusion is judged over the whole tuple of parameters. A pair is valid if the
  equalities that a common value forces cannot hold, or force an instance at which some position
  excludes. A pair that leaves a static parameter free is refused on both paths.
- I never rely on declaration order under walk. I expect "Cannot unify" for an argument outside a bound.
- I do not change code only to pass walk's load check, and do not take its acceptance as proof. I look up
  the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", first.
- I do not write two functional methods with equivalent parameter types at different `self` positions,
  nor an abstract and a concrete one at the same types in one trait. An object that inherits an abstract
  functional method from one trait and its body from another declares the method itself.
- A trait of mine with a functional `+`, `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` gets `excludes { Number }` or
  `excludes { HasRank }`, or I declare the operator in an object. Limit: the checker misses this pair
  against the library (row 918); walk refuses it at load.

### Traits and objects

- No type extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not enforce it, so a walk pass
  proves nothing; I do not copy the Working Draft's "Not allowed" examples.
- I read `comprises` as a statement about values, not as Java's `permits`: a generic trait below a listed
  type need not be listed.
- I write `override` only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than mine. To replace
  at the same types I redeclare without `override`. A wrong `override` in the library stops every walk
  run. Limit: the code generator refuses every `override` (row 650).
- An object covers an inherited abstract method with one body or several narrower ones. Limits: walk
  skips generic objects; the checker refuses a multi-body cover with static parameters (row 725).
- In a self-typed trait I return `self` at the parameter type without a cast. Limit: compiled, such a
  body fails verification (row 695).
- I bound an index parameter with `I extends Index`, but only in code that walk runs or that is checked
  against the interpreter's library; the compiler's prelude has no `Index`. A tuple of `Index` types is
  an `Index`; `()` is not; only `ZZ32` among the integers is. I do not overload a function over `Index`
  with one over a tuple of `Index` types.
- I compare pairs and triples by order only where every element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`, and
  do not order a `List[\RR64\]` in checked code.
- Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is `SEQV`: reference objects, strings among them, only equal
  themselves. I give a value object an `=` to compare by content, do not rely on `=` of tuples longer
  than triples, and write `a <-> b`, not `≡`. Limit: the compiler's library has no `=` over `Any` or
  tuples, and its `===` compares by `=` (row 908).

### Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes

- An unfixed type parameter takes its bound, not `Nothing`. Under walk I write the static argument where
  an inner call needs the outer call's context (`mk[\ZZ64\]()`), and I expect `OPEN` for a self-bounded
  parameter and `Bottom` in three listed cases.
- I use only the three built `where` forms. Another `where` on an `extends` entry is read as
  unconditional, silently. The compiled runtime checks no `where` clause; a compiled call whose clause
  introduces a variable dies (row 867).
- Sizes are equal only when written alike after numeral arithmetic; I do not rely on commutativity
  (`s0 s1` against `s1 s0`), and I expect a `typecase` arm at a numeral to be reachable for a parameter.
  No size power above exponent 4096; no negative exponent.
- A run-time size comes from `reflect`, under walk only. I pass no value of a trait that lists a type at
  a `where`-clause size where the listed type is expected in compiled code (row 307).

### Numbers

- "Tower" in the record does not mean nesting.
- A numeral converts at a typed binding, assignment, field, parameter or declared return type, from its
  exact value; elsewhere it takes `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ` or `RR64`. The default sticks to a variable:
  `x = 0.1; q: QQ = x` is refused. A numeral type is written only as the parameter type of a coercion or
  an operator. A number type of mine takes numerals through a `coerce` generic over the numeral's
  numbers, with a `where` clause for its range; it needs a prefix `-` to take `-3`.
- An all-numeral expression folds exactly before checking, so a test of run-time arithmetic,
  overflow or concatenation needs a variable operand. A folded constant reaches my own type only by a
  coercion from its default type (`coerce(q: QQ)` for `10/20`).
- Coercions apply at calls, typed bindings and assignments; walk skips the declared return type (row 387)
  and does not promote tuple or varargs elements. I expect "Ambiguous coercion" for ties.
- Integer conversion: a checked getter (`x.asZZ32`) to keep the value, a low-bits function (`narrow`, ...)
  to wrap. `ZZ` has only `big`. In compiled code I use only the prelude's listed getters.
- Generic code over `T extends Number` can call nothing on `T`; I declare one function per number type.
  Across types, `=` holds only where a coercion exists; otherwise it is silently `false`, so I write
  `asFloat(x) = y`.
- An integer power keeps its base's type; for a fraction I write `2.0^(-1)` or a `QQ` base. The
  compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32`, `NN64`.
- `/` on integers gives a `QQ`; `DIV` truncates. For a float I make an operand a float, and convert each
  `ZZ64` with `asFloat`. Compiled, `7 / 2` is a static error until the switch-over.

### Reductions and comprehensions

- I write the static argument on `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX`, `BIG MIN` in clause form
  (`SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`), because the checker does not infer it (row 731).
- Under walk without one, the instance comes from a local variable's type or a function's return type,
  not from a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter or an assignment.
- In a reduction of mine without an identity, `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`, never `Any` or untyped;
  I do not copy the team's tests on this.

### Implementation limits

- A walk pass is no type check. I write no `Maybe` as an `if` condition.
- I write every parameter type. A component function without a return type takes the api's.

## 2. Passages that would send a worker wrong, read two ways, or use a term the core lacks

Confidence is that the passage is a real problem for a cold reader.

1. **Numbers, "`Number` declares nothing"**: "To compare a typed value with a numeral, bind the numeral at
   the value's type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then `u = z`. ... the other operand fixes the numeral's
   type, so `u = 0` is `true` for a zero `u: NN32`. Walk departs (`interpreter.md`)." The first sentence
   says a binding is needed; the third says `u = 0` works. I guess the binding is the workaround for
   walk's departure, but the text does not say which path needs it or what walk does. High.
2. **Traits and objects, self-typed, second paragraph**: "Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads
   such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check ... still refuses the
   pair in two cases." "Walk loads" and "walk's load check refuses" stand side by side. The two cases
   cite no ledger row, so by the opening's convention they are not known departures, yet they contradict
   the rule. I cannot tell whether to avoid these two shapes, or to record them. High.
3. **Static parameters, P-48**: "a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside
   `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`." The example shows no bound for `T`, and `(1, 2)`
   would seem to fix `T`. Why `T` is `OPEN` here is not derivable; I would misjudge which calls are
   affected. High.
4. **Static parameters, P-48, list "Walk still gives `Bottom`"**: no action follows. I assume "write the
   static argument", as in the next rule, but it is not said, nor what `Bottom` then does (a failed
   dispatch?). Medium.
5. **Traits and objects, `Index`**: "An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an
   array." The clause does not parse. Medium-high.
6. **Dispatch, row 780**: "walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their
   declared domains only at a call." "Only" attaches to "declared domains" or to "at a call" (not at
   load). Medium-high.
7. **Dispatch, Meet Rule**: "An abstract functional method also counts for it." Counts as an overload
   that needs a cover, or as a declaration that can be the cover? The example suits the first; "Abstract
   declarations count" just above suits either. Medium.
8. **Reductions**: "Write it in every clause form." Of the four named reductions, or of all reductions?
   The next sentence ("Other reductions take their bound") implies the four, but the instruction reads as
   universal. Also the bold sentence "A reduction's static argument depends on the path" states no rule,
   unlike the opening's promise for bold sentences. Medium.
9. **`where` forms**: "Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance
   (row 774)." "Apply" reads as "enforce the condition" or as "extend unconditionally". The list rule
   above (walk orders every list, row 774) suggests the second. Medium.
10. **`override`**: the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650), and walk refuses a
    wrong one. The text does not say whether I may write `override` in the interpreter's library, which
    the compiled path will use after the switch-over, or in a program meant to compile. Medium.
11. **Pairs and triples**: "Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements
    decide ... It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position ... (row 511)." It is not
    clear which sentence row 511 covers, so which is rule and which is departure. "Unordered deciding
    elements give `false`" uses "unordered" for values (NaN?) right after using "ordered" for types.
    Medium.
12. **Opening**: "A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold
    rule." Several cited rows are not that: row 774 names walk and the compiled runtime, row 923 "holds
    the question of longer tuples", rows 441 and 523 sit in an "Until the switch-over" sentence. "Do not
    assert it as correct in a test" also leaves open whether an `XXX` expected failure may assert it.
    Medium.
13. **Dispatch, P-45**: "must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only." Instance
    of which declaration, and how the two instances pair up, is not said. Medium.
14. **Dispatch, P-152**: "a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position,
    so those instances' static arguments are equal." I followed it only through the two examples. The
    sentence alone would not let me judge a new pair. Medium.
15. **`comprises`**: "Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads." The
    step from the value reading to a joint cover is not shown; the same idea is clear in P-147 two
    paragraphs later. Low-medium.
16. **Terms the core does not give, used without a gloss**: `N[\n\]` (in the `typecase` example and
    "the object type `N[\n\]`"), `HasRank` (half glossed as "arrays"), `Vector`, `Matrix`, `array1`,
    `array2`, `AnyIntegral`, `StandardPartialOrder`, `StandardTotalOrder`, `LexicographicOrder`,
    `MINMAX`, `CHOOSE`, "the count stage" (the core names it, but only by pointer), "kind" of a size
    (core gives kinds of static parameters; `nat` against `int` for a size is implied). `N[\n\]` is the
    one that blocks understanding. Medium for `N`, low for the rest.
17. **Numbers, numeral's numbers**: "the digit count, the count of digits after the point, the radix, and
    the digits read as one integer" lists four for a type that has three in `NaturalNumeral`. A reader
    can sort it out from `[\n, m, r, v\]`. Low.
18. **Numbers, fold**: "under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`" and "defaults to a `QQ`" come four
    paragraphs before the sentence that the compiler's library has no `QQ`. Until then "on both paths" in
    the bold rule reads as if the compiled result were a `QQ` too. Low-medium.
19. **`asFloat`**: called a getter by association ("no getters, no `asFloat`"), declared "into `RR64`",
    and written `asFloat(x)`. Whether `x.asFloat` is also valid is open. Low.
20. **Placement**: the rule for `=` and `SEQV` sits under "Traits and objects", and string-literal
    folding under "Numbers". Cross-references exist, but a worker who searches by heading for equality or
    strings misses them. The `Index`, `=` and numeral paragraphs are each one block of fifteen or more
    sentences with several rules and departures; a departure is easy to miss inside. Low-medium.
21. **`Index`**: "In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`"
    comes eight sentences before "write the bound only in code that runs under walk". A worker who stops
    early writes the bound in a program meant to compile. Low-medium.

## 3. Passages that hold repair history, or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding

I found no narrative of past repairs (no batch, date or "was fixed"). The candidates are detail:

1. "The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor." The
   descriptor is in the core ("The compiled runtime"); neither half changes what I write.
2. "Walk has no static types. ... So walk runs programs that the checker refuses." The core says this in
   "How a program runs". Only the `Maybe` condition is new.
3. Reductions: "Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a
   top-level or local function's return type" and "Else walk takes the join" repeat the core's "Static
   parameters" bullet. The new parts are "also where the clause form ends a block" and the list of what
   does not direct it.
4. "The number types are flat siblings (P-43)" repeats the core; its paragraph earns its place only by
   the gloss of "route A" and "the tower".
5. Self-typed, second paragraph: "With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ..., the library's
   generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own." This
   justifies a state of the library. It changes an action only if a worker would otherwise report that
   pair as invalid; if that is the purpose, say so.
6. "Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same
   limits." A pointer with no content here; one clause would do.
7. "The class loader computes a size without checking its kind" — the action is in the second half
   (a negative exponent stops with a Java exception, row 675).
8. "`NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, which lists a type at a `where`-clause
   size." It explains the cause; the next sentence carries the rule for my own traits.
9. "The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place
   reuses it (P-176)." I can name no action it changes, unless the type is a reference object and
   identity matters; the text does not say.
10. "A chain of `||` folds character literals too, if its first or second operand is a string literal."
    The action ("a test of run-time concatenation needs a variable operand") holds without it.
11. "An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, 'body param 1'" and
    "fails with 'Cannot unify'": diagnostic strings. They help me recognise a failure; they change no
    choice. Keep if recognition is the aim.
12. "Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`": tells me nothing
    to do differently, unless old code uses those getters.

1	<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->
2	
3	# Writing the skills
4	
5	The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.
6	
7	## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else
8	
9	A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
10	- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
11	- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."
12	
13	## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them
14	
15	A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
16	- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
17	- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."
18	
19	## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest
20	
21	Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
22	- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
23	- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"
24	
25	## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work
26	
27	A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
28	- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
29	- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."
30	
31	Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.
32	
33	## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name
34	
35	A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
36	- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
37	- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."
38	
39	## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace
40	
41	The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
42	- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
43	- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."
44	
45	Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.
46	
47	## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read
48	
49	A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
50	- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
51	- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."
52

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- A numeral at `=` takes its default. So `u = 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q = 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 973). `u =/= 0` and `q =/= 0.5` are then `true` (ledger row 966). Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u = z` or `u =/= z`.
- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).
- A numeral type written as a static argument, or as a type that an object or a trait extends, loads and runs, as `Wrap[\NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\]\](3)` does (ledger row 974). The rules refuse both forms, as the compiled checker does: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.

Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).

  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`;
- names, in a `builtinPrimitive` string, a helper that walk refuses ("Natives").

Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.

In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:

- a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own;
- the library's objects that extend number types, not the glue classes of the same names: `Int` (`ZZ32`) in `int`, `Long` (`ZZ64`) and `UnsignedLong` (`NN64`) in `long`, and `BigNum` (`ZZ`) in `BigInteger`.

A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the first list: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- The binding is in a method of a type that the second list does not name, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the lists, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

The check has two gaps:

- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads. A call of a method of `ZZ32` that binds a helper then stops with 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (ledger row 551).

A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. A `||` of string literals folds into one literal, a `FlatString`, so a test that needs a `CatString` joins a literal with a variable. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.

# The interpreter (walk)

Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:

- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
- `glue/`: the natives.

## How walk evaluates a program

After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.

At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.

Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. Walk has no static types, so it cannot choose statically. The expected-failure tests `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss` and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC.fss` record the difference.

Walk departs from the rules of `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", in these ways, until each fix lands. A test of one of these cases asserts the rules' answer, as an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`), unless the case says otherwise.

- A float numeral to the left of an `RR32` operand runs `RR64`'s operator: for `a: RR32`, `2.5 + a` is an `RR64`, and `a + 2.5` an `RR32` (ledger row 958). Bind the numeral at `RR32` first, as `c: RR32 = 2.5`, then write `c + a`.
- A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).
- A `nat` or `int` parameter of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` (ledger row 962). Assert no value for it in a test.
- A numeral at `=` takes its default. So `u = 0` is `false` for a zero `u` of `NN32`, `NN64` or `RR32`, and so is `q = 0.5` for `q: QQ = 1/2` (ledger row 973). `u =/= 0` and `q =/= 0.5` are then `true` (ledger row 966). Bind the numeral at the type first, as `z: NN32 = 0`, then write `u = z` or `u =/= z`.
- A numeral that rounds to an infinity at `RR32` or `RR64` gives `Infinity`, with no error (ledger row 967).
- A numeral type written as a static argument, or as a type that an object or a trait extends, loads and runs, as `Wrap[\NaturalNumeral[\1, 10, 3\]\](3)` does (ledger row 974). The rules refuse both forms, as the compiled checker does: 'NaturalNumeral cannot be written in a program except as a parameter's type.'
- A body with a declared return type is not converted by coercion, except a numeral: `r(): Wide = NarrowOf(3)` returns the `NarrowOf` (ledger row 387). Write the value at the declared type.

## Where a fix of walk belongs

Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:

- coercion;
- chained comparisons;
- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.

Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if walk is wrong on one of these nodes, fix the evaluator, not the desugarer.

An edit of a phase that both paths run, or of the desugaring switches, can change both paths. An edit under `interpreter/` changes walk only.

## What walk checks

Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). The commands that stop after a phase, and `unparse`, use the compiler's prelude and the compiled path's desugaring switches (`compiler.md`, "The `fortress` commands"). So `fortress typecheck` does not check a walk program, and `desugar` or `unparse` does not print the tree that walk runs. That tree is the component's entry in `interpreter_cache/` (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

Under walk, the disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses a program's own top-level type that has the name of a type of `FortressLibrary`, such as `Index` or `Indexed`: "Type name may refer to: Index, FortressLibrary.Index". Give such a type another name.

At load, walk checks the overload sets, some `comprises` clauses, inherited abstract methods and `override` declarations. It lifts each object expression to the top level as an object, which takes the static parameters of an enclosing generic function, and checks it as an object. It checks a trait or object with static parameters once, through a stand-in: one type for all its instances, with a symbolic type for each static parameter (`symbolicInstance` in `interpreter/evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`). Through the stand-in, it does not check two functional methods whose parameter types mention a symbolic type. It makes no stand-in, and so checks nothing through one, for a declaration with an `opr` static parameter, or where its static parameters, `where` clause or `extends` clause raise an error at the symbolic types. It refuses:

- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap. For every pair of functions of which at least one is generic, it checks the overloading rules of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", on their declared domains (`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading"): the No Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule. So it refuses two whose declared domains are equal. The message names the rule: "fails because their parameter lists have the same types", "fails the Return Type Rule" or "fails the Meet Rule". Walk keeps the team's check and messages for the pairs below. The team's check looks for a position where the two parameter types neither nest nor exclude. If a parameter type there mentions a static parameter, the message is "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types". If neither does, it is "are unrelated (neither subtype, excludes, nor equal) and no excluding pair is present". The pairs:
  - a pair with a varargs parameter;
  - a pair whose parameter lists differ in length, only where one of them has a varargs parameter. Walk checks no other pair of lists of different lengths;
  - a pair that is neither two generic declarations, nor a generic one beside a plain one, nor a generic function beside a generic trait's or object's functional method that has no static parameters of its own;
  - the instances of an explicit instantiation.

  Where it reads exclusion over the whole tuple of parameter types, at the instance that the equalities force, it reads two parameter types that still mention a static parameter as excluding only where no instances of the two can meet. Walk departs from the rules in these cases:
  - At load, it does not check two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains. It compares them at each call, on the instance that the call makes. So such a pair that breaks the rules loads, and a call can fail with "Cannot find definition for method" (ledger row 780).
  - It refuses two generic functional methods whose declared domains lie one inside the other, in a type without static parameters (ledger row 779).
  - It refuses a pair whose overlap it finds only through an instance of a supertype, also where a third declaration covers the overlap (ledger row 539).
  - It refuses overloads on two instantiations of one generic type, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])` (ledger row 416).
  - Its parameter-by-parameter check reads an object type over a static parameter as excluding a type that one of its instances is or extends. So it loads `g[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: ZZ32)` beside `g(x: Box[\ZZ32\], y: Any)`, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 788).
  - It reads no `where` clause when it reads exclusion over the whole tuple. So it refuses such a pair where one declaration has a `where` clause of its own (ledger row 787).
  - It does not refuse a type that extends a self-typed trait `T[\A\]` and is not an `A` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). A call that both `T`'s operator and another declaration fit then runs one of them, without an ambiguity error (ledger row 893). Make each type that extends `T[\A\]` an `A`.
  - It loads a generic top-level function whose declared domain lies inside that of a self-typed trait's functional method of the same name, where the Return Type Rule holds. The checker refuses every top-level function more specific than a functional method of its name, a check that the specification does not state: '… is more specific than the declaration of the functional method' (ledger row 894).
  - It loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it, which the Meet Rule refuses (ledger row 806).
  - It loads a type that provides two functional symbolic operators, such as two `||`, that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`). The checker refuses the pair (ledger row 611).

  The paths differ on `f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T)` beside `f(x: Z)`, where `K comprises { A, B, C }`, `Z excludes { A, B }`, and `C` is an object that extends `Z` but not `R`. Walk refuses the pair: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker reads the bounds, finds that no value lies in both domains, and accepts it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 713).
- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods in a type that provides both, where their name is an identifier or an operator named by a word, as `MAX`.
- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses. Where a listed type names a bounded type `where`-clause variable, as `NBox[\E\]` in `comprises { NBox[\E\] } where [\E extends Number\]`, walk ignores the variable's bound, and runs `NBox[\String\]` (ledger row 754). In another declaration's bound, it takes a name equal to the variable's as the variable (ledger row 778).
- a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, where a member's declared type names the variable: "Missing type E" (ledger row 755).
- an object or object expression without static parameters that inherits an abstract method and does not define it. Bodies define it if they are at or below its parameter types and together cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk also refuses where its search for a cover does not settle: at a cycle of `comprises` clauses, at a symbolic type, or beyond 10,000 steps or 4,096 combinations of listed types. It also refuses a valid object whose one body for the method has a static parameter of its own (ledger row 728).
- a declaration with the modifier `override`, in a trait, object or object expression, that overrides no declaration that its type's immediate supertraits provide. An `override` at an inherited declaration's own parameter types overrides nothing. At an instance of a generic trait above a declared object, equal parameter types count as overridden. Walk does not read all the bounds of the static parameters in two cases:
  - an object expression, which takes its static parameters from the function around it;
  - a generic trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause.

  In these cases, walk does not refuse an `override` if the inherited declaration's parameter types mention a static parameter and differ from the `override`'s.

So a library edit can stop every program at load, if it does one of these:

- adds an overload;
- leaves an inherited abstract method that no bodies cover, covers it only by a body with a static parameter of its own, or covers it by bodies whose cover walk's search cannot settle;
- adds an `override` that overrides nothing;
- gives a member a type that names its trait's `comprises`-clause variable, as `E` in `AnyList`;
- names, in a `builtinPrimitive` string, a helper that walk refuses ("Natives").

Walk checks a program's declarations against the library's only when it analyses the library, not when it loads the library's entries from the cache (ledger row 342). So a program that walk refuses with an empty cache runs with a filled one. Deleting the program's own entries does not bring the check back. To see such a refusal, run with an empty cache, as `COLD_CACHE=1` gives `harness-one.sh`.

Walk compares no component with the apis that it exports. So a component that leaves out an api member, or declares it at another header, loads and runs under walk. The compiled export check refuses it (ledger row 841). `library.md`, "Designing a change", gives the step that runs the check on each component.

`tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.

Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.

## Natives

The library binds each of walk's natives by a declaration whose body is `builtinPrimitive("…")`. The string names one of these:

- A glue class, as `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X`, in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. A glue class takes walk's `FValue` objects, so the compiled path cannot use it.
- A helper: a public static method of a class under `nativeHelpers/`, as `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.<method>`. `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java` calls it by reflection, with a method's `self` first. The compiled path calls it too (`compiler.md`, "Natives"). Most bindings name a helper. The others name a glue class. F-299 counts both kinds (`records.md`, "Reading the record").

Walk carries each declared type of a helper's binding in one Java type:

- `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `Char` in `int`; `ZZ64` and `NN64` in `long`; `RR64` and `Float`, the library's object that extends `RR64`, in `double`; `RR32` in `float`; `Boolean` in `boolean`;
- `FlatString` and `JavaString` in `String`, and `String` too, except as a parameter other than `self`; `ZZ` in `BigInteger`; `()` in `void`; `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader`, the library's writer and reader traits, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedWriter` and `FortressBufferedReader`, which the checker reads back as the two traits.

In a method, walk carries `self` by the type that declares the method:

- a type of the list above, except `JavaString` and `()`, in the same Java type, but `FlatString` only where it is the library's own;
- the library's objects that extend number types, not the glue classes of the same names: `Int` (`ZZ32`) in `int`, `Long` (`ZZ64`) and `UnsignedLong` (`NN64`) in `long`, and `BigNum` (`ZZ`) in `BigInteger`.

A program can give its own type the name `FlatString` or `JavaString`. Walk tells the library's `FlatString` by the component that declares it, so a program's own type of either name carries no `self`. But walk carries a parameter declared at such a type in `String`, by the type's name alone, and does not refuse the binding. The native then receives the name of the type, not the value's text (ledger row 877). Give a program's own type another name.

Walk refuses a helper's binding at load in these cases. The message names the string, and contains the words below, which a `load_exception_contains` key can match:

- The class or the method does not exist: 'not found' or 'names no static method of'.
- The result type, or a parameter type other than `self`'s, is not carried by the first list: 'no Java type carries the declared'.
- The binding is in a method of a type that the second list does not name, as a program's own object: 'no Java type carries T, the type of self.', with the type's name as T. Match ', the type of self.' to tell it from the refusal above.
- No method of that name, or more than one, has exactly the Java types of the lists, with `self`'s first in a method: 'has no overload that fits the declaration's types', or 'overloads that fit'.

The check has two gaps:

- Walk checks the binding of a dotted method of a generic trait or object only when the program makes an instance, at run time. So a program that makes no instance loads. One that makes an instance stops there with the same message, as an `InterpreterBug` (ledger row 864). Test such a binding with a program that makes an instance.
- Walk reads the type that declares the method, not the type of the value. So a program's object that extends `ZZ32` loads. A call of a method of `ZZ32` that binds a helper then stops with 'getInt not implemented for FOrdinaryObject' (ledger row 551).

A glue class bound over `String`, and a helper bound in a method of `String` as `self`, receive the wrong text for a `CatString`: the name of the type, not its characters (ledger row 846). `||` builds a `CatString` when the joined string is longer than `maxLeafSize`, 32 characters by default. A `||` of string literals folds into one literal, a `FlatString`, so a test that needs a `CatString` joins a literal with a variable. Bind such a native over `FlatString`, and beside it an overload over `String` that passes `s.asFlatString`, as `printlnWithThread` does (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4640-4644`). In a method of `String`, call that overload with `self`.

An `import java` written in a `.fss` file is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it. The compiled path's generated `import java` (`compiler.md`, "Natives") is not this one.

A glue class raises a Fortress exception that a `catch` sees by throwing a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `interpreter/glue/prim/Int.java` makes one, and its callers throw it:

    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
    return new FortressError(f);

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

## Running a program

    bin/fortress P.fss

- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/claude_demo.fss`. It prints `SUM[i <- 1#100] i = 5050` among its lines, and exits 0. `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.

## The model program

MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. Check the model when your brief asks for it: run your tree's `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. `<work-dir>` is a folder under your tree's `tmp/`, and `threads` sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, 1 by default. The script runs the quick pair at once, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`: two forward and backward passes each, against the reference values, in about 56 s for both. Each starts from an empty private cache and writes `<work-dir>/<name>.txt`. Read its `VERDICT:` line and its last line, `rc=`.

- Add the word `full` only if your brief asks for it. It runs the full pair, `MicroGptFlatCheck.fss` and `MicroGptAplCheck.fss`, with 40 checks each and a 90-minute timeout.
- If you change a line of the model, put the change in your report as a diff.
